claims.claim: The same essay argues Martin prioritizes rhythm and momentum over sentence polish, so description is forgettable while dialogue excels.
claims.source: At Sea Journal, 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer' (undated)

claims.claim: A hostile reviewer lists 'jape' and 'mummer's farce' among words Martin rides like a hobbyhorse, and calls the prose at best serviceable.
claims.source: The Erstwhile Philistine, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin' (2012-03-21)

claims.claim: The same reviewer finds the sex scenes reliant on clichés such as 'drunk with desire'.
claims.source: The Erstwhile Philistine, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin' (2012-03-21)

claims.claim: 'Words are wind' appears thirteen times in A Dance with Dragons across every region and faction, which the essay reads as deliberate motif.
claims.source: Overthinking It, 'Words are Wind: Repetition of Language in A Dance With Dragons' (2011-08-17)
claims.quote: no writer uses a phrase thirteen times by accident

claims.claim: Commenters on that essay counter that Martin has a penchant for pseudo-archaic language and, once he likes a term ('much and more', 'leal'), uses it everywhere.
claims.quote: GRRM has a penchant for pseudo-archaic language

claims.claim: The same thread credits Martin with strong leitmotifs, notably Reek's rhyme refrain.
claims.quote: he does do leitmotifs extremely well

claims.claim: A lexicographer notes 'ser', 'southron' and 'craven' are 15th-century forms and 'turncloak' is Martin's coinage from 'turncoat'.
Recurring sayings ('Dark wings, dark words', 'Words are wind', 'Seven hells') characterize cultures, and dialogue stays in English with culture-specific idiom rather than invented tongues.
Grossman characterizes Martin by sudden reversals and a plotter's tension, with narration shot from many angles by a dozen narrators.
Grossman ties the multi-narrator scheme to the gritty, many-sided politics, which he calls all real.
claims.quote: Martin shoots the action from many angles, with a dozen narrators

claims.feature: epic sweep with small human drama (praise)
claims.claim: Grossman praises Martin's ability to hold epic sweep and tiny, touching human drama in the same frame.
claims.quote: epic sweep and tiny, touching human drama

claims.claim: Brown finds too much repetition, unexceptional prose, and characters who share idioms regardless of class or continent.
David Orr in the NYT argued the books' length is unnecessary and damages both prose and plot mechanics; Wasson in the CSM called the prose concise but pithy.
claims.source: Wikipedia, A Dance with Dragons, Reception (aggregator citing NYT 2011-08-14 and CSM 2011-07-12)
claims.quote: it hurts Martin's prose and his plot mechanics

claims.claim: Hartinger calls the prose tight, clear and evocative and the individual chapter structure about as good as structure gets, faulting only scope.
claims.quote: about as good as structure gets

claims.feature: food as character and region marker (critic)
claims.claim: Mikanowski reads soup descriptions as regional and moral markers, with honorable men sharing soup.
claims.quote: Honorable men share their soup. Bad ones bogart it

verdicts.note: Verbatim as 'The con: The sentences aren't beautiful.' Essay also supplies each supporting limb: 'he stresses rhythm'; stock phrases are 'Very important for maintaining momentum'; 'dialogue would shine brightest. But the prose that constitutes the other 60% of the text is forgettable.' Title confirmed 'George R.R. Martin, The American Homer'.

verdicts.trueWording: words and phrases he rides like a hobbyhorse
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: 'He has words and phrases he rides like a hobbyhorse'. 'jape' is item 1 and "mummer's farce" item 2 in the list that follows. The 'at best serviceable' limb is a light paraphrase of the page's 'Most of the time his prose borders on the servicable' (misspelled in the original); the word 'serviceable' correctly spelled does not appear.

verdicts.trueWording: someone being drunk with desire for the other person
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim inside 'They usually involve someone being drunk with desire for the other person, their head swimming with the wine of lust or some such nonsense.' Caveat: 'cliche' is the summarizer's word, not the author's — he writes 'clunky to the extreme' and 'the obligatory mention of naughty body parts'; 'cliches' appears only in reader comments.

verdicts.trueWording: no writer uses a phrase thirteen times by accident
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim ('Again, no writer uses a phrase thirteen times by accident.'). Count verbatim too: 'The phrase "words are wind" appears thirteen times in ADWD.' 'Every region and faction' is a fair compression of 'people in the North, the South and on both sides of the Narrow Sea… Everyone says it.'

verdicts.trueWording: I think GRRM has a penchant for pseudo-archaic language
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the comment by 'Wenyip' (Aug 17 2011), which also names 'much and more' (and 'little and less') and cautions against reading much into 'leal'. Minor: it is one commenter, not 'commenters' plural, and the tone is a caveat rather than a counter-argument.

verdicts.trueWording: On the other hand, he does do leitmotifs extremely well
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the same Wenyip comment, which continues 'My especial favourites were the two for Reek: "Reek, Reek it rhymes with…"', confirming the Reek-refrain detail.

No quote field to check. Page: 'Ser for Sir, Southron for Southern, and craven meaning cowardly all date from 1451, 1488, and 1400 respectively, according to the Oxford English Dictionary' and 'turncloak, which is Martin's archaic-sounding amendment of turncoat'. Two drifts: craven's 1400 is 14th-, not 15th-century, so '15th-century forms' overreaches for one of the three; and Adam Pulford is described on the page as working 'in marketing for Oxford Dictionaries', not as a lexicographer.

Quote verbatim; 'Words are wind' and 'Seven hells' both appear in the same 'The power of proverbs' section, tied to culture ('the seven kingdoms of Westeros contain many'). The invented-tongue limb is verbatim too: 'the tongue in which they are speaking is noted but rendered in English', against Tolkien-style 'fully developed fantasy languages'.

verdicts.trueWording: George R.R. Martin is fond of sudden reversals
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim as the article's opening sentence. Plotter limb verbatim: 'Martin is a tense, surging, insomnia-inflicting plotter'; many-angles limb verbatim as in claim 324. Article fetched in full (not paywalled).

verdicts.trueWording: Martin shoots the action from many angles, with a dozen narrators
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, continuing '…the better to reflect its gritty, twisty, many-sided nature'. The 'all real' limb is verbatim but about politics specifically, spelled 'politik': 'Martin may write fantasy, but his politik is all real.'

verdicts.trueWording: epic sweep and tiny, touching human drama
verdicts.note: Verbatim inside 'Martin has an astonishing ability to focus on epic sweep and tiny, touching human drama simultaneously.'

Verbatim in the reviewer's preamble to the interview: 'Weaknesses that have plagued Martin's previous books are also present: too much repetition, unexceptional prose, and characters who use the same idioms (and have sex in exactly the same manner) no matter their ethnicity, social class, or continent.' Byline Rachael Brown, July 11, 2011.

verdicts.trueWording: Such length isn't necessary, and it hurts Martin's prose and his plot mechanics
verdicts.note: Both halves verbatim on the Wikipedia reception section: Orr quoted as above, and 'Megan Wasson of The Christian Science Monitor said… Martin's prose is concise but pithy'. One date drift: the article's own citation dates Orr to August 12, 2011 ('Dragons Ascendant: George R. R. Martin and the Rise of Fantasy'), not the 2011-08-14 in the source field; the CSM date (July 12, 2011) matches.

verdicts.trueWording: The structure of the individual chapters is often about as good as structure gets
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the prose limb is verbatim too, with the original's typo: 'He prose is tight and clear and evocative'. 'Faulting only scope' is a slight narrowing — his fault is that Martin 'seems to have lost complete control of his overall story' and traded story for 'atmosphere', of which length is one symptom. Post dated May 05, 2014, itself a repost of a 2012 piece.

verdicts.trueWording: Honorable men share their soup. Bad ones bogart it.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, immediately preceded by the two markers the claim names: 'It's a marker of regional difference. It's a test of character.' By Jacob Mikanowski, July 05, 2017.
